<section class="page-hero"><h1>Chùa Bút Tháp (Ninh Phúc tự 寧福寺)</h1><p class="lead">Bút Tháp · Bắc Ninh, Vietnam</p></section>
<main class="content"><div class="content-inner fieldwork-story sakya-story but-thap-story">
<figure class="fieldwork-hero"><img src="/assets/images/but-thap-01.webp" alt="A doorway frames one of the monastery’s long brick-paved passages." loading="lazy"><figcaption>A doorway frames one of the monastery’s long brick-paved passages.</figcaption></figure>
<p class="lead">Bút Tháp, whose formal name is Ninh Phúc tự 寧福寺, is one of the most important surviving Buddhist architectural and sculptural ensembles of northern Vietnam. Its origins are traditionally traced to the Trần period, but the monastery seen today is above all the product of a major seventeenth-century reconstruction. That distinction matters: Bút Tháp is not simply a medieval foundation preserved unchanged, but a site in which an older sacred history was materially reshaped during the Lê Trung Hưng period.</p>
<figure class="fieldwork-figure-wide"><img src="/assets/images/but-thap-09.webp" alt="The stone Bảo Nghiêm tower, one of Bút Tháp’s visual signatures." loading="lazy"><figcaption>The stone Bảo Nghiêm tower, one of Bút Tháp’s visual signatures.</figcaption></figure>
<p>The monastery became especially prominent in the seventeenth century under the Zen master Chuyết Chuyết (1590–1644), a major figure of the Lâm Tế lineage in Vietnam. After his abbacy, aristocratic patronage supported an ambitious rebuilding campaign. The surviving complex remains unusually coherent: a long axial sequence of gates, halls, courtyards, the bell tower, sanctuaries and rear buildings is enclosed and linked by extended corridors. The stone Bảo Nghiêm tower, associated with Chuyết Chuyết, gives the complex one of its most distinctive vertical accents.</p>
<div class="figure-pair"><figure><img src="/assets/images/but-thap-10.webp" alt="Timber architecture and tiled roofs within the monastic compound." loading="lazy"><figcaption>Timber architecture and tiled roofs within the monastic compound.</figcaption></figure><figure><img src="/assets/images/but-thap-11.webp" alt="Stone bridge, lotus pond and the long wooden hall." loading="lazy"><figcaption>Stone bridge, lotus pond and the long wooden hall.</figcaption></figure></div>
<p>The architecture is inseparable from sculpture. Carved timber, stone balustrades, altars, ritual furnishings and statuary create a dense visual environment in which seventeenth-century craftsmanship survives on an exceptional scale. The official heritage inventory records nearly one hundred statues. Among them are groups of Buddhas, Manjuśrī (Văn Thù) on the lion, Samantabhadra (Phổ Hiền) on the elephant, protective figures and portrait images.</p>
<figure class="fieldwork-figure-wide"><img src="/assets/images/but-thap-08.webp" alt="Courtyard, incense burner and timber hall beneath mature trees." loading="lazy"><figcaption>Courtyard, incense burner and timber hall beneath mature trees.</figcaption></figure>
<p>The long corridors and successive thresholds also change the way the images are encountered. Rather than being isolated as museum objects, sculptures appear within a sequence of ritual spaces, incense, dark timber interiors and controlled light. Bút Tháp therefore preserves not only individual masterpieces but also the spatial setting that gives them devotional meaning.</p>
<figure class="fieldwork-figure-wide"><img src="/assets/images/but-thap-04.webp" alt="The thousand-armed and thousand-eyed Quan Âm, completed in 1656." loading="lazy"><figcaption>The thousand-armed and thousand-eyed Quan Âm, completed in 1656.</figcaption></figure>
<p>At the centre of Bút Tháp’s fame stands the monumental “Thousand-Armed and Thousand-Eyed” Quan Âm (Avalokiteśvara), completed in 1656 by the sculptor Trương Thọ Nam. About 3.7 metres high, the image combines a frontal, meditative body with an extraordinary radiating field of arms and eyes. Its technical ambition, iconographic complexity and exceptional state of preservation have made it one of the canonical masterpieces of Vietnamese wood sculpture; it is now recognized as a National Treasure.</p>
<div class="figure-pair"><figure><img src="/assets/images/but-thap-02.webp" alt="A large protective figure within Bút Tháp’s sculptural ensemble." loading="lazy"><figcaption>A large protective figure within Bút Tháp’s sculptural ensemble.</figcaption></figure><figure><img src="/assets/images/but-thap-06.webp" alt="A row of gilded Buddha images within the sanctuary." loading="lazy"><figcaption>A row of gilded Buddha images within the sanctuary.</figcaption></figure></div>
<p>Seen together, the statues show the breadth of Bút Tháp’s visual programme. Calm Buddha images, dynamic guardians, bodhisattvas, portrait-like figures and elaborate devotional sculpture occupy the same complex. Their surfaces—gilded, lacquered, darkened by age or illuminated only intermittently—make clear how much the experience of Buddhist art depends on architecture and light.</p>
<div class="figure-pair"><figure><img src="/assets/images/but-thap-03.webp" alt="A seated figure preserved in the dim interior." loading="lazy"><figcaption>A seated figure preserved in the dim interior.</figcaption></figure><figure><img src="/assets/images/but-thap-05.webp" alt="A portrait-like seated figure, lit from the side." loading="lazy"><figcaption>A portrait-like seated figure, lit from the side.</figcaption></figure></div>
<figure class="fieldwork-figure-wide"><img src="/assets/images/but-thap-07.webp" alt="A gilded seated figure among the temple’s historic images." loading="lazy"><figcaption>A gilded seated figure among the temple’s historic images.</figcaption></figure>
<p>For the history of Buddhist art, Bút Tháp is therefore valuable on several levels at once: as a Trần-period foundation, as a major seventeenth-century Lê Trung Hưng reconstruction, as a centre associated with Chuyết Chuyết, and as a rare ensemble in which architecture, sculpture and ritual setting are still legible together. The site offers a concentrated view of the technical and devotional sophistication reached by Vietnamese Buddhist art in the seventeenth century.</p>
<section class="fieldwork-notes"><h2>Reference points</h2><ul><li><strong>Origins:</strong> Trần dynasty; later major seventeenth-century reconstruction.</li><li><strong>Location:</strong> Bút Tháp, Bắc Ninh, south bank of the Đuống River, Vietnam.</li><li><strong>Key figure:</strong> Zen master Chuyết Chuyết (1590–1644).</li><li><strong>Major work:</strong> Thousand-Armed and Thousand-Eyed Quan Âm, 1656, Trương Thọ Nam.</li><li><strong>Coordinates:</strong> approx. 21.06103° N, 106.02225° E.</li></ul></section>
</div></main>
